references.text: The preceding parable about the unjust judge and the widow, which Jesus now comments on in verse 6. The Lord urges the disciples to pay attention to what "the unjust judge" says ([ref:Luk 18:1-5|Luke 18:1-5]).

Jesus draws a conclusion from the unjust judge's behavior to God's behavior: If even an unjust judge gives in, how much more will God secure justice for his chosen ones ([ref:Luk 18:7-8|Luke 18:7-8]).

A similar argument "from the lesser to the greater" appears in the parable of the friend who knocks at night: here too, the point is that persistence in prayer leads to an answer ([ref:Luk 11:5-8|Luke 11:5-8]).

Abraham appeals to God as the judge of all the earth and asks: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" The contrast with the unjust judge is clear — God is righteous ([ref:1 Mos 18:25|Genesis 18:25]).
"He is the Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just." God's righteous character stands in sharp contrast to the unjust judge ([ref:5 Mos 32:4|Deuteronomy 32:4]).
The psalmist asks whether judges truly judge righteously — the theme of unjust earthly judges runs throughout Scripture ([ref:Sal 58:2|Psalms 58:2]).

A command to help the fatherless and defend the widow's cause, showing God's care for vulnerable groups — the widow in the parable represents precisely those whom God wants to protect ([ref:Jes 1:17|Isaiah 1:17]).
Woe to those who enact unjust laws and deny justice to the helpless — again the theme of unjust judges who deny righteousness ([ref:Jes 10:1-2|Isaiah 10:1-2]).

The martyrs under the altar cry out: "Lord, you holy and true one, how long before you judge and avenge our blood?" Here too, the theme is persistence and crying out to God for justice ([ref:Åp 6:10|Revelation 6:10]).
